Game company executives are often surprisingly out of touch with their product's most dedicated and skilled user bases. They erroneously believe that their mistake was in trying to monetize the products of an established modding community on a game that had been out for a long time. However, if they try it out of the gate with the next TES title, they are likely to have a hard time for a couple reasons. First, it'll be the same modding community. Many Oblivion modders moved to Skyrim, and things are already pretty well established. Second, very few of the more complex mods are created in a vacuum. There is a lot of resource sharing by a lot of different people that occurs, and the currency is recognition and respect, not dollars, because the dollars wouldn't be enough for the time and effort that went into it to be anything but symbolic anyway. What won't go over well will be offering a fraction of those dollars to one person and nothing to the rest and assuming people will like that because, heck, it's more than what they were doing it for before, right?

I'm not averse to them putting paid mods into future games but they need to solve two things:

1) Discovery, so that the mod marketplace doesn't get spammed to shit with endless weapon packs or whatever in place of quality content.

2) Have it declared from the start, rather than springing it on a mod community a few years after release.

I'd happily pay ten bucks for something like Falskaar, and if the marketplace managed to create more of those I'd be happy. I wouldn't happily pay ten bucks for some reskins and weapon packs.

Curation should be fairly obvious. Anyone can make a mod for Skyrim. I made my own follower in an afternoon. Was it worth $1? Fuck no. It was just a custom follower that wouldn't permanently die. Steam (LOL) or Bethesda would need to actually look at each mod that wanted to be monetized and determine whether it should be allowed to make money.

Communication, again, should be fairly obvious. The paid mods thing came out of nowhere, and if I recall correctly, even the modders weren't given much notice that they'd need to make a whole new mod for the system.

Reliability, I feel, is my most important one. Modders drop support for their mods all the time. Is Bethesda going to take over updating mods that were abandoned? Or are they going to refund people when the mod starts breaking? And then there's compatibility; is Bethesda going to work to make sure all paid mods can work together with no issues? Or at least provide modders with the tools to make it an easier process?

I'd still be pretty wary if/when Bethesda tries paid mods again, but I honestly think unless they wait a decade or more that people will still throw a fit in response.
